title: How Long Do Drains Stay In After a Tummy Tuck?
meta_description: Usually 1 to 2 weeks, removed once the fluid slows. How tummy tuck drains work, how to empty them, what removal feels like and drainless options.
excerpt: Tummy tuck drains usually come out in 1 to 2 weeks, once the fluid slows. What they do, how to empty and record them, what removal feels like, and when a drainless tummy tuck is an option.
quick_answer:
How long do drains stay in after a tummy tuck?

Usually 1 to 2 weeks (Cindy Wu, MD) or 7 to 10 days, sometimes 2 weeks or longer (Paul Vitenas, MD), both on the ASPS website; The Aesthetic Society gives 3 to 14 days. They come out once the fluid slows, so your surgeon sets the day from your output and exam.

How to empty and measure a drain

Wash your hands.
Open the stopper and pour the fluid into a measuring cup.
Write down the amount for each drain, with the date and time.
Squeeze the bulb flat, then replace the stopper.
Secure the bulb so it does not pull on the tubing.
Wash your hands again.

When it is about half full, usually every 4 to 6 hours for the first few days.

Source: Cleveland Clinic

Source: Cleveland Clinic.

sources.title: Answers to common tummy tuck questions
quotes: If a drain is placed, then it will be removed as soon as the output is low enough (usually in 1-2 weeks).
You will be bent at the waist while standing or lying down for 7-10 days after surgery to protect the incision and to allow for your skin to adapt.
The bruising will subside in a couple of weeks, and the swelling will continue to diminish until approximately three months post-procedure.

sources.publisher: ASPS website, a post by Paul Vitenas, MD
sources.title: Five things to consider before getting a tummy tuck
quotes: In most cases, the drains are painlessly removed in seven to ten days, however, they may need to stay in place for two weeks or longer.

sources.title: Tummy Tuck - Aftercare & Recovery
quotes: Your surgeon will typically remove your drains three to fourteen days after your surgery, depending on how much fluid is coming out.
Depending on the extent of your tummy tuck, you may have tubes in your incision to drain away fluid.
Other red flags include shortness of breath, chest pains, and an unusual heartbeat.

sources.title: Jackson-Pratt (JP) Drain
quotes: You’ll need to empty the bulb when it’s about halfway full.
In general, you’ll need to do this every four to six hours the first few days until the amount decreases.
A fever of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius) or more.
Redness, swelling, warmth or increased pain at the site.
Drainage that’s smelly, green, milky white or thick.
The drainage increases for two days straight (it should be decreasing).
The fluid returns to a dark or bright red after lightening (this is a sign that you’re bleeding).
Pale yellow (straw color) or clear: Drainage that goes from red to pale yellow or clear is a sign you’re healing.
Don’t pin the drain to your pants or belt loops.
Sometimes, after providers remove JP drains, fluid collects and swells at the surgical site (wound). This fluid is called a seroma. This isn’t an emergency, but you should alert your provider.

sources.publisher: Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open
sources.title: Final 24-hour Drain Output and Postoperative Day Are Poor Indicators for Appropriate Drain Removal (Chua and colleagues, 2022)
quotes: Of the 1308 patients, 616 had a drain and a complete record.
Our data suggest neither postoperative day nor 24-hour volume before drain removal are valid indicators for removal.
A retrospective chart review was conducted for surgical operations performed by our division

sources.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Evaluating the Surgical Outcomes of Progressive Tension Suturing Compared to Drains in Abdominoplasty Surgery (G. Rao and colleagues, 2024)
quotes: Closed suction drains are placed to prevent seroma formation after abdominoplasty, but evidence of their effectiveness is limited, and they may increase infection risk and patient discomfort.
PTS significantly reduced postoperative seroma rates (relative risk [RR] 0.34; 95% CI 0.15-0.76; P = .001)
compared to drains, with no significant differences in hematomas, infections, or dehiscence.
The review included 24 studies with 750 patients, including 2 randomized controlled trials,
Larger, high-quality studies are needed to further assess the safety and efficacy of drainless abdominoplasty.
